claims.text: The baseline magnetic high-entropy alloy is homogeneous and single-phase.
The baseline alloy has relatively few intrinsic domain-wall-pinning defects.
Annealing the alloy at elevated temperature can place it in a two-phase region.
Rapid quenching after annealing can freeze nanoscale precipitates into the alloy.
The proposed heat treatment will produce nanoscale precipitates distributed throughout the alloy matrix.
Precisely controlled treatment temperature and duration can ensure uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates.
Effective domain-wall pinning requires precipitates with an appropriate size and density.
Nanoscale precipitates act as domain-wall-pinning centers.
Precipitate-induced pinning increases the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
The increased pinning hinders magnetic-domain reversal.
Hindering magnetic-domain reversal raises the coercive field relative to an untreated homogeneous alloy.
When precipitate formation is optimal, the heat-treated alloy will show a statistically significant increase in coercive field relative to a matched untreated baseline.
Precipitates that are too coarse or too sparse may fail to increase coercivity.
The heat-treatment parameters and resulting precipitate characteristics vary with alloy composition.
TEM can be used to assess the presence, size, and distribution of the targeted precipitates.
VSM measurements can compare coercive fields between heat-treated and untreated sample sets.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the expected coercivity increase to samples in which suitable precipitates actually form, but the falsification rule treats failure to form those precipitates as falsification of the coercivity mechanism. That outcome instead indicates unsuccessful implementation of the specified intervention and is not a decisive test of whether formed precipitates increase coercivity.
